effect: An AI government that is losing the public now listens to it more, most of all before an election. The AI weighed public opinion in its choice of laws by electoral integrity x (0.15 + 0.45 x election nearness) and in its budget by (0.4 + integrity x (0.6 + nearness)), and the nearness term also eased tightening before a vote; approval never entered, so a government at 20% approval 90 days before a vote acted exactly like one at 70%. Now the nearness term these rules read is nearness x (1 + risk) + 0.25 x risk, where risk = (45 - approval) / 20, clamped 0 to 1 (zero at 45% approval and above, full at 25% and below): a losing government near a vote gives public opinion up to about twice the weight, and one far from a vote a little more (0.25 x risk) than none; a country with no election scheduled gets no far-from-a-vote term. The pull that eases budget tightening is capped at 1 as before, and it still vanishes under market pressure (the game multiplies it by 1 - fiscal pressure), so a government in a debt crisis is not let off. Electoral integrity multiplies every term, so regimes without real elections are unchanged. Real-world behaviour: governments trailing in the polls before an election spend more, cut taxes and drop unpopular bills (political budget cycles; from memory). Day-0 effect: none (every accountable regime starts at 48% approval or more, measured on day 2 of a new game, so risk is 0); it is live within months, as approval falls: by day 120 on seed 12345 about 32 accountable countries are under 45%, among them the United States at about 40%. No new saved state.
